Because each hidden state strictly depended on the computation of the immediately preceding hidden state, parallelization across modern GPU clusters was mathematically impossible. Furthermore, as sequence lengths exceeded several hundred tokens, the gradients propagated backward through time suffered from exponential decay or explosive numerical instability, effectively blinding recurrent networks to long-range context.

When researchers first attempted to model complex dynamic systems, they relied on deterministic heuristics and rigid symbolic logic. But as the sheer scale and dimensionality of real-world information overwhelmed hand-crafted rules, the scientific community realized that intelligence could not be hard-coded; it had to be learned through continuous optimization across high-dimensional parameter spaces. For every token, the model calculates three distinct linear projections using learned weight matrices: a Query vector representing what information the token is seeking, a Key vector representing what information the token holds, and a Value vector containing the actual semantic payload. The affinity between any two tokens is determined by computing the inner dot product of their respective Query and Key vectors. In high-dimensional vector spaces, this dot product computes the cosine similarity: vectors pointing in convergent directions produce large positive scalars, indicating high mutual relevance.

The raw attention energy matrix S is computed as S = (Q K^T) / sqrt(d_k). The scaling factor 1 / sqrt(d_k) is mathematically essential: assuming components of Q and K are independent random variables with zero mean and unit variance, their dot product has a mean of zero and variance of d_k. Without scaling, the variance scales linearly with dimension, driving the softmax outputs toward extreme one-hot vectors with near-zero gradients.
